rv.q: Too British? Not if you want to laugh uproariously — and perhaps even unexpectedly shed a tear or two.
Operation Mincemeat is totally lovable and expertly zany, with Big Let’s Put on a Show Energy.

Operation Mincemeat isn't exactly blazingly clever—the jokes fly thick and fast, and they tend toward broad grin-crackers rather than breathless zingers—but it overflows with good humor and heartfelt commitment.
Audiences are always receptive to flights into jubilant escapism—perhaps particularly now—and this plucky musical provides it in generous doses.

Juvenile silliness is the blood pumping through this show. It’s packed with visual gags, mocking quirks and vocal modulations. Though not the quickest way to my funny bone, it totally works for general delight-seeking Broadway audiences
I enjoyed “Operation Mincemeat” well enough, but I would have enjoyed it much more if I thought that were true onstage.

As Malone delivers it, with beautiful directness in a wistful high tenor, the troubles of the real world take center stage and the troubles of the show melt away. Like Hester herself, it’s the quietly beating heart of the whole operation.
I found the story absorbing; the yuks, abusive.
This ripping yarn is a lot of fun and very clever to boot.
I'll be surprised if, even in this season of Broadway musical theater, the Operation Mincemeat itself doesn't pick up a slew of nominations and awards.
Operation Mincemeat is some of the best of what musical theatre can be.
The wartime spoof from comedy troupe SpitLip is an undeniable success.
Even if its sense of British humor is not your cup of tea, it’s hard not to be in awe at its comedic and dramatic audacity.
Operation Mincemeat is a highlight of the season.

Be it further known that SpitLip’s Operation Mincemeat, one of those transfers where pre-shipping worries go like “Is it too British?” is quite British but is also unremittingly tough, ultimately adorable, and joyfully welcome. Some readers of this extremely favorable review will think the title is vaguely familiar.
Operation Mincemeat is a must-see show for you.
There's still an air of fringiness to the venture, and it is a bit bloated, taking quite a lot of time in the first act to get its footing before finally soaring like a runaway balloon.
The show's focus skis all over the place, slaloming from hilarity to dense plot explanation to deeper meditations on patriotism, sexism, and loss.
Indeed, given everything at stake, the show's flippant tone -- often reminiscent of an extended Monty Python sketch -- can feel a little unsettling.
David Bergman's virtuosic video design and Snook's riotous rollercoaster of a 26-part performance keep The Picture of Dorian Grey riveting and compellingly ridiculous.

If it ultimately feels too clever by half, that may be because this new musical by comedy troupe SpitLip, opening on Broadway tonight, is different in a crucial way from, say, “Monty Python’s Spamalot” or Mystery Theater Company’s “That Goes Wrong.”
Whether its humor is for you, only you can decide.
Nothing kills a laugh faster than seeing actors sweat.
And with that, Operation Mincemeat, the new musical, finds the exact right formula for hilarity and loving engagement, telling a near-perfect tale in the most inventive theatrical fashion.
Operation Mincemeat isn’t just an exercise in turning history into a glorified pop concert, à la Six , or spoofing real events with the broad strokes o...

All the madness comes together rather spectacularly in a show that proves that crazy-crackers outside-the-box creative ideas can beat the Nazis and can also make for a truly terrific and sometimes sublime theatrical experience.
Both arrive with clarity and purpose, and both serve as reminders of what the Broadway musical, carefully wrought, can accomplish.
With jazzy ear-worms and a poignant showstopper, Mincemeat is supremely entertaining. The ensemble is indefatigable, the stagecraft is inventive and the slapstick sublime.
This production shines most brilliantly when it takes itself a bit more seriously.

cn.t: This clever British musical spoof about a WWII deception operation charms critics with its energetic cast of five playing dozens of roles, witty humor, and surprising heart, though some find its frenetic style exhausting and too clever by half.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
